items.title: Scalar-vector potential pairs, gauge transformation, Lorenz divergence and the wave expression
items.reference: definition-contracts.md#def-em-gauge-transformation and definition-contracts.md#def-em-retarded-point-geometry (locally constructed mathematical vocabulary; recorded in the batch notes)

items.statement:
Let $c>0$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ be open. A **scalar-vector potential pair** of class $C^k$ on $\Omega$, for an integer $k\ge1$, is a pair $(\varphi,A)$ with $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ each of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], the components of $A$ being of class $C^k$ separately; the pair is **smooth** when both members are $C^\infty$, and **continuous**, or of class $C^0$, when both members are continuous. A pair defined on a set of the form $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ with $t_0<T$ is of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, **in the extension sense** when there are an open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ and a potential pair of class $C^k$ on the open set $\mathbb R^3\times J$ whose restriction to $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ the given pair is; the same wording is used for $C^\infty$ and for the single functions $\varphi$ and $\chi$ below.

All operators $\nabla$, $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\Delta$ below act on the three spatial coordinates with $t$ fixed: for $\Omega_t:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:(x,t)\in\Omega\}$, apply the cited three-dimensional operators to the restrictions $x\mapsto\varphi(x,t)$, $x\mapsto A(x,t)$ or $x\mapsto u(x,t)$ on the open set $\Omega_t$. In particular $\nabla\varphi=(\partial_{x_1}\varphi,\partial_{x_2}\varphi,\partial_{x_3}\varphi)$ and $\Delta u=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}^2u$; $\partial_t$ differentiates only the time coordinate.

For a potential pair of class $C^k$ with $k\ge1$ its **electric field** and **magnetic field** are

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Both $E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(\varphi,A)$ are maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$.

For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is the function

$$G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi,$$

also of class $C^{k-1}$, and the pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega$ when $G(\varphi,A)=0$ throughout $\Omega$.

For $k\ge2$ and a function $\chi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^k$, a **gauge function**, the **gauge transform** of the pair is

$$T_{\chi}(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

again a potential pair, of class $C^{k-1}$.

Finally, for a function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$ put

$$Wu:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2u-\Delta u,$$

with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and $\partial_t^2$ the second partial derivative in $t$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); this is the normalization $W=c^{-2}\Box_c$ of the wave operator $\Box_c=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$ of speed $c$ of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]. For a map $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ of class $C^2$ with components $U_1,\dots,U_m$, one writes $WU:=(WU_1,\dots,WU_m)$ componentwise.

Nothing in this definition asserts that a gauge function with prescribed auxiliary data exists, that every potential pair is gauge equivalent to a pair in Lorenz gauge, or that $Wu=g$ is solvable: those are conclusions with their own hypotheses. The signs $-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $A+\nabla\chi$, the factor $c^{-2}$ in $G$, and the spelling *Lorenz* are part of the convention.
items.strategy: Vocabulary and regularity audit; a definition asserts no existence theorem. (i) If $\varphi,A$ are $C^k$ then $\nabla\varphi$ and the three partial derivatives $\partial_tA_i$ are $C^{k-1}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so $E(\varphi,A)$ is a $C^{k-1}$ map $\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ and likewise $B(\varphi,A)$ and $G(\varphi,A)$ for $k\ge1$, since the curl and divergence of a $C^1$ field are computed pointwise from first partial derivatives ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). (ii) For a $C^k$ gauge function with $k\ge2$, $\partial_t\chi$ and $\nabla\chi$ are $C^{k-1}$, so $T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ is a pair of class $C^{k-1}$. (iii) The wave expression is the stated normalization: [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]] fixes $\Box_c=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$, so $c^{-2}\Box_c=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta=W$, and $\Delta$ is the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. (iv) No solvability is asserted: existence of $\chi$ with $W\chi=G$ is supplied later on this page under slab hypotheses, and it carries the Axiom of Countable Choice through the cited wave theorem. The definition is stated on an arbitrary open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ so that both the full slab and complements of worldlines are instances.

items.title: The retarded wave kernel is a distribution supported on the cone, solves the point-wave equation, and convolves to the retarded solution
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the sphere and polar integrations below ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]). Let $c>0$, write $Q:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, $\mathcal D:=\mathcal D(Q)$ for the test-function space of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], and $C:=\{(y,t)\in Q:t=|y|/c\}$ for the retarded cone. Define the functional $K$ on test functions by $$\langle K,\psi\rangle:=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\psi(y,|y|/c)}{|y|}\,dy\qquad(\psi\in\mathcal D).$$ Then: (a) the integral converges absolutely for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$, the functional $K$ is a distribution on $Q$ ([[def-distribution]]), $(K,\psi)=0$ for every $\psi$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap C=\varnothing$, and for every $(y_0,t_0)\in C$ and every neighbourhood $U$ of $(y_0,t_0)$ there is $\psi\in\mathcal D$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq U$ and $\langle K,\psi\rangle\ne0$; consequently $\operatorname{supp}K=C$. (b) For every $h\in C_c^\infty(Q)$ the function $$(K*h)(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{h(y,\,t-|x-y|/c)}{4\pi\,|x-y|}\,dy$$ is well defined (the integral converges absolutely), of class $C^\infty$ on $Q$, and for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$ $$\langle K*h,\psi\rangle=\langle h,\,K\circledast\psi\rangle,\qquad (K\circledast\psi)(y,s):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,s+\cdot)\rangle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\frac{\psi(y+z,s+|z|/c)}{|z|}\,dz;$$ moreover $W(K*h)=h$ on $Q$ in the classical pointwise sense, where $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ is the wave expression of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. (c) Read $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ as the distributional operator built from [[def-distributional-derivative]]; then $WK=\delta_{(0,0)}$ in the sense of [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]], that is, $(WK)(\psi)=\psi(0,0)$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$. This identifies $K$ as the retarded fundamental solution of $W$; no smoothness of $K$ itself on the cone is asserted, and the advanced fundamental solution is not treated.
items.strategy: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. (a) Well-definedness and continuity: fix $\psi\in\mathcal D$ with support in a compact set, choose $R>0$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq B_R(0)\times[-R,R]$ ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), and let $M:=\sup|\psi|<\infty$ on the compact support ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]). Then $|\langle K,\psi\rangle|\le\frac{M}{4\pi}\int_{B_R}|y|^{-1}dy$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]), and by [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] applied to the nonnegative Borel function $y\mapsto|y|^{-1}\mathbf 1_{B_R}(y)$, with $d\sigma$ the polar measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], $\int_{B_R}|y|^{-1}dy=\int_0^Rr^{-1}\sigma(S^2)r^2\,dr=\tfrac12\sigma(S^2)R^2<\infty$. Hence the integral converges absolutely and the bound is a fixed-support seminorm of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]] on each $\mathcal D_K$, i.e. $K$ is continuous for the LF topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]: $K\in\mathcal D'$. Support: if $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap C=\varnothing$ then $\psi(y,|y|/c)=0$ for every $y\ne0$, so the integrand vanishes off the null set $\{0\}$ and $\langle K,\psi\rangle=0$. Conversely fix $(y_0,t_0)\in C$ and a neighbourhood $U$. If $y_0\ne0$, take a nonnegative bump $\psi$ supported in a small ball inside $U$ about $(y_0,t_0)$ with $\psi(y_0,t_0)>0$: by continuity $\psi(\cdot,|\cdot|/c)$ is positive on a neighbourhood of $y_0$, a set of positive measure, and $|y|^{-1}$ is bounded there, so $\langle K,\psi\rangle>0$ ([[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]], [[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]]). If $y_0=0$, then $t_0=0$ and $\psi(y,t)=\rho(|y|)\eta(t)$ with nonnegative bump factors supported in a small ball about the origin inside $U$ and positive at the origin gives $\langle K,\psi\rangle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\rho(|y|)\eta(|y|/c)|y|^{-1}dy>0$ by the same positivity argument. Hence no point of $C$ is outside the support and $\operatorname{supp}K=C$. (b) For fixed $(x,t)$ the defining integral converges absolutely: if $\operatorname{supp}h\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)\times[-\rho,\rho]$ and $(y,t-|x-y|/c)\in\operatorname{supp}h$, then $y\in\overline B_{\rho+|x|}(0)$; $|h|\le\|h\|_\infty$ and $1/(4\pi|x-y|)$ is integrable over that compact ball by the same polar computation, so [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] gives absolute convergence. Pairing identity: substitute $x=y+z$ in the $x$-integral and $t=s+|z|/c$ in the $t$-integral (two translations of Lebesgue measure, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]) and interchange the $y$- and $(z,t)$-integrations with [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] (absolute integrability follows by bounding h and psi and enclosing the contributing y,s,z in a bounded cylinder; the only pole is 1/|z|, whose integral over a bounded ball is finite by the preceding polar calculation; continuity at the pole is neither true nor required): $\langle K*h,\psi\rangle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int h(y,s)\Bigl[\int\frac{\psi(y+z,s+|z|/c)}{|z|}dz\Bigr]dyds=\langle h,K\circledast\psi\rangle$, the inner bracket being exactly the definition of $K$ applied to the test function $(z,u)\mapsto\psi(y+z,s+u)$ (its support is compact). Identification with the wave solution: let $h\in C_c^\infty(Q)$ and $t_0$ below the time support of $h$. Apply [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] with $a=b=0$ and source $h$ on the slab $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$, $T$ above the time support: its solution is $u(x,t)=c^2\int_{t_0}^tH_{h(\cdot,v)}(x,t-v)\,dv$ with $H_\varphi(x,s)=sM_{cs}\varphi(x)$, $M_{r}\varphi(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{S^2}\varphi(x+rn)\,d\Omega(n)$. Writing the sphere average as an integral over the sphere and using [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] on the compact rectangle $[t_0,t]\times S^2$, the substitution $r=c(t-v)$ with the absolute derivative ([[cor-one-dimensional-change-of-variables-with-absolute-derivative]]) turns the integral into $u(x,t)=\int_0^{c(t-t_0)}r\,\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{S^2}h(x+rn,t-r/c)\,d\Omega(n)\,dr$. The chart surface measure on $S^2$ agrees with the polar measure $\sigma$ ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], $n=3$), so applying [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] to the nonnegative Borel function $y\mapsto|h(x+y,t-|y|/c)|(4\pi|y|)^{-1}\mathbf 1_{|y|\le c(t-t_0)}$ (and passing to positive and negative parts, [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]) gives $u(x,t)=\int_{|y|\le c(t-t_0)}\frac{h(x+y,\,t-|y|/c)}{4\pi|y|}\,dy$; the omitted range $|y|>c(t-t_0)$ has $t-|y|/c<t_0$, where $h=0$. After the reflection $y\mapsto-y$ this is $(K*h)(x,t)$ on the whole slab. Since for every point $(x_*,t_*)\in Q$ one can choose a slab $[t_0,T]$ containing it with $t_0$ below and $T$ above the time support of $h$, [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] gives $Wu=h$ at that point and $K*h=u$ there; hence $K*h$ (well defined on all of $Q$ and smooth on every slab) is $C^\infty$ on $Q$ and $W(K*h)=h$ pointwise. (c) Let $\eta\in C_c^\infty(Q)$ be a nonnegative bump with $\int\eta=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\eta\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$ and let $\eta_\varepsilon$ be its mollifier family ([[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]], [[def-l-one-approximate-identity-on-rn]]). By (b), $W(K*\eta_\varepsilon)=\eta_\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. For bounded continuous $\varphi$, $\langle\eta_\varepsilon,\varphi\rangle\to\varphi(0)$: convolve with the reflected bump and apply [[cor-l-one-approximate-identities-converge-uniformly-on-compacta-for-continuous-functions]] at the origin. Hence for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$, $\langle K*\eta_\varepsilon,\psi\rangle=\langle\eta_\varepsilon,K\circledast\psi\rangle\to(K\circledast\psi)(0,0)=\langle K,\psi\rangle$, because $K\circledast\psi$ is continuous (its defining integral is dominated by $2\|\psi\|_\infty/(4\pi|z|)$ on a compact $z$-set, so [[thm-dominated-convergence]] applies as $(y,s)\to(0,0)$), i.e. $K*\eta_\varepsilon\to K$ in the weak topology of $\mathcal D'$. The distributional operator $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ is a continuous linear map on $\mathcal D'$ for the weak topology, being a finite linear combination of derivatives, each of which is continuous linear ([[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]); therefore $WK=W(\lim_\varepsilon K*\eta_\varepsilon)=\lim_\varepsilon W(K*\eta_\varepsilon)=\lim_\varepsilon\eta_\varepsilon=\delta_{(0,0)}$ in $\mathcal D'$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]). No smoothness of $K$ on the cone is claimed or used. For the approximate-identity application in (c), F(y,s)=(K circledast psi)(y,s) is bounded on ALL parameter space: if the spatial projection of supp psi lies in B_M with M>0, the contributing z lie in B_M-y. For |y|<=2M this is contained in B_3M and its |z|^-1 integral is finite; for |y|>2M one has |z|>=|y|-M>M and the integral is bounded by |B_M|/M. Multiply by ||psi||infinity/(4pi). Continuity on every bounded parameter neighborhood follows from the same fixed compact-z polar majorant and dominated convergence. Thus the stated bounded-continuous approximate-identity interface is actually applicable.

items.title: Every smooth potential pair on a slab can be put in Lorenz gauge by a wave-equation gauge function, without changing the fields
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), carried through [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] and its sphere integrations ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $t_0<T$, and let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of class $C^\infty$ on the slab $Q:=\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]: $\varphi$ and $A$ are restrictions of $C^\infty$ functions on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ for some open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Put $G:=G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$ and $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$. Then: (a) there is a gauge function $\chi:\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense with $\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$, $\partial_t\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$ and $W\chi=G$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$; (b) the gauge-transformed pair $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\,A+\nabla\chi)$ is again of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense and its fields are unchanged: $$E(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=E(\varphi,A),\qquad B(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=B(\varphi,A)\qquad\text{on }Q;$$ (c) the transformed pair is in Lorenz gauge: $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=G-W\chi=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$; (d) if $\chi_1,\chi_2$ are of class $C^2$ on $Q$ in the extension sense and $W\chi_1=W\chi_2=G$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, then $W(\chi_1-\chi_2)=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$. Nothing is asserted about prescribed boundary values of $\chi$ on a bounded spatial domain, about spatial decay of $\chi$, or about Lorenz gauge fixing for a cavity problem with prescribed boundary data; the older global gauge promise on bounded domains is outside this result.

items.title: The smooth forced Maxwell Cauchy system on a slab: existence, uniqueness, Gauss constraints and the c-cone of dependence
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) through [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c,\varepsilon,\mu>0$ with $\varepsilon\mu c^2=1$, let $t_0<T$, and let $\rho:\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ and $J:\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense (restrictions of $C^\infty$ functions on $\mathbb R^3\times I_{\rm ext}$ for some open interval $I_{\rm ext}\supset[t_0,T]$, [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) satisfying the continuity equation $$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0\qquad\text{on }\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T).$$ Let $E_0,B_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfy $\operatorname{div}E_0=\rho(\cdot,t_0)/\varepsilon$ and $\operatorname{div}B_0=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$. Then: (a) the first-order system $$\partial_tE=c^2\operatorname{curl}B-\frac{J}{\varepsilon},\qquad \partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E\qquad\text{on }\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T),$$ with $E(\cdot,t_0)=E_0$, $B(\cdot,t_0)=B_0$, has exactly one solution $(E,B)$ with $E,B$ of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense; (b) this solution obeys both Gauss laws on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$: $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon$ and $\operatorname{div}B=0$; (c) (domain of dependence) if $(\tilde\rho,\tilde J,\tilde E_0,\tilde B_0)$ is second data of the same kind and, for some $x_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and $t_*\in(t_0,T]$, one has $\tilde E_0=E_0$, $\tilde B_0=B_0$ on the closed base ball $\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$ and $\tilde\rho=\rho$, $\tilde J=J$ on the closed backward cone $K(x_*,t_*)=\{(y,v):|y-x_*|\le c(t_*-v),\ t_0\le v\le t_*\}$ ([[def-forward-and-backward-wave-cones-domain-of-dependence-and-influence]]), then $\tilde E(x_*,t_*)=E(x_*,t_*)$ and $\tilde B(x_*,t_*)=B(x_*,t_*)$. This is a statement about the stipulated smooth system with coefficients and sources given; no physical identification of $(E,B)$ with an electromagnetic field, no finite-domain boundary problem and no decay at spatial infinity is asserted.

items.title: Retarded Liénard-Wiechert potentials and fields of a uniformly subluminal smooth point source
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*<c$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}\subseteq\Omega$. For $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ let $s=s(x,t)$ be the unique retarded root of [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]] with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and put $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|>0$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$, $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$, $N:=n\cdot\beta$, $D:=\kappa r$, $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ and $d:=n\cdot\dot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then: (a) the scalar distribution $\rho\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ and the vector distribution $J\in(\mathcal D'(\Omega))^3$ of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]], $$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)\,\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,$$ satisfy $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. (b) Let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] and, for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and $\tau\in\mathbb R$, $y\in\mathbb R^3$, put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$. Define the retarded-history pairings by the explicit integrals
$$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad
\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds.$$
Here the second integral is componentwise. The notation $\varepsilon_0^{-1}\langle\rho,K\circledast\psi\rangle$ and $\mu_0\langle J,K\circledast\psi\rangle$, if used, means precisely these explicit history integrals, rather than ordinary distribution action on a compactly supported test. These pairings define distributions on $\Omega$, are finite for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and satisfy the exact retarded-convolution identities $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta(x,t)}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt$$ (for $\Upsilon$, componentwise against $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$; both integrands are continuous on the open set $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and integrable there against $\psi$). Consequently the potentials are the $C^2$ functions $$\varphi:=\frac{C}{D}=\frac{C}{\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R,\qquad A:=\frac{\beta\,\varphi}{c}=\frac{\beta\,C}{c\,\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R^3$$ off the worldline, and the zero extensions $\widetilde\varphi,\widetilde A$ on $\Gamma$ belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$; $\Phi$ is the regular distribution of $\widetilde\varphi$, and $\Upsilon$ that of $\widetilde A$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function|regular distribution]]). (c) Let $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]). Then, off the worldline, $$E=C\left[\frac{(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2}+\frac{n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r}\right],\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}.$$ The fields $E,B$ are $C^1$ off the worldline. More generally, if $z\in C^k$, $k\ge3$, the retarded root is $C^k$, the potentials are $C^{k-1}$ and the fields are $C^{k-2}$ there; if $z\in C^\infty$, all these objects are smooth off the worldline. The result is a mathematical model computation for the stipulated uniformly subluminal smooth worldline and the retarded choice; no self-force law, no radiation-reaction postulate and no physical Maxwell coupling is asserted or proved.
items.strategy:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as stipulated in the statement. (a) Apply [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] to the $C^1$ curve $z$ on $\mathbb R$; $C^3$ is a special case, and its all-time graph is proper because a compact ambient set bounds the time coordinate.
(b) Fix a compact observation set $Q\subseteq\{(x,t):|x|\le M,\ t_0\le t\le t_1\}$, and tests supported in $Q$. If $g(s,y):=(z(s)+y,s+|y|/c)\in Q$, then $s\le t_1$. For $s\le0$, using $|z(s)|\le Z+v_*|s|$ with $Z:=|z(0)|$ gives
$$t_0\le s+|y|/c=s+|x-z(s)|/c\le -(1-v_*/c)|s|+(M+Z)/c.$$
Thus $s\ge-S$, where $S:=\max\{0,(M+Z-ct_0)/(c-v_*)\}$. If $[-S,t_1]$ is empty no contributing point exists. Otherwise set $H:=\max(S,|t_1|)$ and $L:=1+M+Z+v_*H$. Every contributing $y$ has $|y|\le M+|z(s)|<L$. Consequently the pulled-back support lies in the bounded closed cylinder $[-S,t_1]\times\overline B_L$, possibly approaching $y=0$; it need not be compact inside $U:=\mathbb R\times(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$.
On that cylinder, $|\psi(g(s,y))|/(4\pi|y|)\le\|\psi\|_\infty/(4\pi|y|)$. The polar formula [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] gives $\int_{B_L}|y|^{-1}dy=\sigma(S^2)L^2/2<\infty$. Borel product identification [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]] and the Euclidean/product-measure bridge [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] allow [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] for the absolute value. Then [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] identifies the double integral with the explicit iterated history integral. In particular, with $T:=\max(0,t_1+S)$ and $M_Q:=T\sigma(S^2)L^2/(8\pi)$,
$$|\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle|\le |q|M_Q\|\psi\|_\infty/\varepsilon_0,\qquad
|\langle\Upsilon_j,\psi\rangle|\le\mu_0|q|v_*M_Q\|\psi\|_\infty.$$
The seminorm $\psi\mapsto|\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle|$ restricts continuously to each fixed-support test space by these bounds, and likewise for each component of $\Upsilon$. Thus [[def-test-function-topology]] and [[def-distribution]] prove distribution continuity directly; no action of $\rho$ or $J$ on a noncompact test is assumed.
The graph $\Gamma$ is closed: convergence of $(z(s_j),s_j)$ forces $s_j\to t$ and $z(s_j)\to z(t)$. Thus $V:=\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ is open. On $U$, $g$ is $C^1$, and in coordinate order $(s,y_1,y_2,y_3)$ its determinant is $-\kappa(s,y)$, with $\kappa=1-(y/|y|)\cdot z'(s)/c\ge1-v_*/c>0$. If $g(s,y)=g(s',y')$, then $|s-s'|=||y'|-|y||/c\le|z(s')-z(s)|/c\le(v_*/c)|s-s'|$, so $s=s'$ and $y=y'$. No image point belongs to $\Gamma$: otherwise $|y|=|z(t)-z(s)|\le v_*(t-s)=v_*|y|/c$, contradicting $y\ne0$. Conversely every point of $V$ has the unique retarded root supplied by [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]], giving inverse $(x,t)\mapsto(s(x,t),x-z(s(x,t)))$. Its $C^1$ regularity follows from that supplier's $C^3$ branch on the open domain $x\ne z(t)$, using this consumer's $C^3$ hypothesis. No exclusion of the entire spatial trajectory is imposed. Therefore $g:U\to V$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism.
For any compact $Q\subseteq\Omega$, the nonnegative Borel substitution lemma [[lem-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-borel-functions-via-radon-uniqueness]] applied to $1_Q/(\kappa r)$ on $V$ yields
$$\int_V\frac{1_Q}{\kappa r}\,dx\,dt=\int_U\frac{1_Q(g(s,y))}{|y|}\,ds\,dy<\infty.$$
The same bound holds for $|\beta|/(c\kappa r)$ since $|\beta|\le v_*/c$. Extend the potentials by zero on the closed graph. These extensions are Borel and locally integrable on all of $\Omega$. Applying the same Borel substitution first to the absolute value of $\psi/(\kappa r)$ establishes its $L^1$ integrability on $V$, and [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]] then gives the scalar pairing formula in the statement. Apply it componentwise to $z'(s)$-weighted data for the vector formula. Its prefactor is
$$\frac{\mu_0qz'(s)}{4\pi\kappa r}=\frac{\mu_0qc\beta}{4\pi\kappa r}=\frac{\mu_0c\varepsilon_0 C\beta}{\kappa r}=\frac{C\beta}{c\kappa r},$$
since $\mu_0c^2\varepsilon_0=1$. The regular-distribution identities mean the zero extensions, as in [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]; tests may be nonzero on $\Gamma$. The retarded root is $C^3$ on $V$, and $r,n$ are $C^3$ while $\beta,\kappa,D$ are $C^2$ with $D>0$, so the potentials are $C^2$. The same composition argument gives the matching $C^k$ and $C^\infty$ branches.
(c) Derivatives of the retarded data: from $t-s=r/c$ and R1, $\nabla s=-n/(c\kappa)$, $s_t=1/\kappa$, hence $\nabla r=n/\kappa$ and $r_t=-cN/\kappa$ (chain rule, [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); $R=x-z(s)$ gives $\partial_iR=e_i+\beta\,n_i/\kappa$ and $\beta=z'(s)/c$ gives $\partial_i\beta=-\dot\beta\,n_i/(c\kappa)$, while $\beta_t=\dot\beta/\kappa$ (componentwise chain rule and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). Since $D=r-R\cdot\beta$, the product rules for the Euclidean pairing give $D_t=r_t-R_t\cdot\beta-R\cdot\beta_t=(c(|\beta|^2-N)-rd)/\kappa$ and $\partial_iD=\partial_ir-(\partial_iR)\cdot\beta-R\cdot\partial_i\beta$, hence $\nabla D=((1-|\beta|^2+rd/c)/\kappa)\,n-\beta$; the required product rules are the coordinatewise one-variable product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then $\varphi=C/D$ gives $\nabla\varphi=-C\nabla D/D^2$, $\varphi_t=-CD_t/D^2$, and $A=\beta\varphi/c$ gives $A_t=(\beta_t\varphi+\beta\varphi_t)/c=\dot\beta C/(c\kappa D)-\beta CD_t/(cD^2)$, so $$E=-\nabla\varphi-A_t=\frac{C}{D^2}\Bigl(\nabla D+\frac{\beta D_t}{c}\Bigr)-\frac{C\dot\beta}{c\kappa D}.$$ The bracket equals $\frac{(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)+(rd/c)(n-\beta)}{\kappa}$ (substituting the two displayed identities and $\kappa=1-N$), and writing the second term over the common denominator $\kappa^3r^2$ replaces its numerator by $-r\kappa\dot\beta/c$, giving $E=\frac{C}{\kappa^3r^2}\bigl[(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)+\frac{r}{c}\bigl(d(n-\beta)-\kappa\dot\beta\bigr)\bigr]$; the coordinate triple-product identity $n\times((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta)=d(n-\beta)-\kappa\dot\beta$ (expand both sides with [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]) yields the displayed $E$. For the magnetic field, $\operatorname{curl}(\beta\varphi/c)=\nabla(\varphi/c)\times\beta+(\varphi/c)\operatorname{curl}\beta$ ([[lem-divergence-and-curl-are-linear-and-obey-the-scalar-product-rules]]), and $\operatorname{curl}\beta=\nabla s\times\dot\beta$ by the coordinate formula applied to $\beta=z'(s(x,t))/c$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); substituting $\nabla\varphi=-C\nabla D/D^2$ and $\nabla s=-n/(c\kappa)$ gives $$B=-C\left[\frac{1-|\beta|^2+rd/c}{c\kappa D^2}\,n\times\beta+\frac{n\times\dot\beta}{c^2\kappa D}\right].$$ Crossing the displayed $E$ with $n/c$ gives this same expression by $n\times(n-\beta)=-n\times\beta$ and $D=\kappa r$, proving $B=n\times E/c$. Both displayed fields are $C^1$ off the worldline, and no derivative of $z$ beyond the third order and no bound on $\Gamma$ at infinity is used; the caveats in the statement are exactly those of the research branch argument.

items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let c>0, epsilon0>0, q in R, mu0=(epsilon0 c²)^-1, and let z:R->R³ be C³ with |z'(s)|<=v*<c for all s. These are mathematical parameters. On Q=R³ times R let rho,J and Phi,Upsilon be exactly the proper point-current and retarded-history distributions of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] and [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]], with the kernel K of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] and no independent free addition. Put W=c^-2 partial_t²-Delta. Then (a)
$$W\Phi=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad W\Upsilon=\mu_0J,\qquad \operatorname{div}\Upsilon+c^{-2}\partial_t\Phi=0\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(Q).$$
(b) Define the vector distributions $\mathcal E=-\nabla\Phi-\partial_t\Upsilon$ and $\mathcal B=\operatorname{curl}\Upsilon$ using componentwise [[def-distributional-derivative]] and the usual finite-coordinate cross/curl convention [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. They satisfy
$$\operatorname{div}\mathcal E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\quad\operatorname{div}\mathcal B=0,\quad\operatorname{curl}\mathcal E=-\partial_t\mathcal B,\quad\operatorname{curl}\mathcal B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_t\mathcal E.$$
(c) On the complement of Gamma={(z(s),s)}, these distributions restrict to the exact C1 Lienard-Wiechert fields of the earlier point-potential lemma, with all its higher-regularity branches retained. The zero extensions of those E,B formulas on Gamma belong to L1loc(Q), and their regular distributions are precisely mathcal E,mathcal B ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]). The off-worldline C1 fields also satisfy the source-free classical Maxwell equations there, because the point pair restricts to zero and each continuous regular residual is zero. Thus the equations in (b) are equations for locally integrable fields with the exact point source, not merely arbitrary field distributions. No field value on Gamma is physically assigned; zero extension is a representative convention on a null set. No physical adoption, nonlinear distribution product, finite self-energy, self-force, global acceleration bound, or incoming-field uniqueness theorem is asserted.
items.strategy:
Use only the existing explicit histories, not an undefined convolution of two noncompact distributions. Fix psi in D(Q) with observation support |x|<=M,t0<=t<=t1. The earlier point-potential proof gives a common proper-history cylinder [-S,t1] times B_L for every contributing (s,y), where S=max(0,(M+|z(0)|-ct0)/(c-v*)) and L=1+M+|z(0)|+v*max(S,|t1|); derivatives of psi have the same observation support. All relevant absolute integrals are bounded by a derivative supremum times integral over that cylinder of 1/|y|, finite by [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], with the actual nonnegative order rules [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]. If the history interval is empty all pairings vanish.
For F(y,s)=(K circledast psi)(y,s), each parameter derivative is K circledast the corresponding test derivative. Indeed on a bounded parameter neighborhood, the spatial projection of psi's support confines the kernel variable to one bounded ball; every difference quotient is dominated by its test-derivative supremum times |w|^-1 there. Dominated convergence [[thm-dominated-convergence]] and the scalar FTC show F is smooth and give those identities for all derivatives. For each fixed (y,s), translation of WK=delta from [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] yields (K circledast Wpsi)(y,s)=psi(y,s). Apply this pointwise identity inside the bounded absolute history integrals: <Phi,Wpsi>=q/epsilon0 integral psi(z(s),s)ds and <Upsilon_j,Wpsi>=mu0 q integral z'_j(s)psi(z(s),s)ds, proving the two distributional wave equations, including q0.
The function s->F(z(s),s) is C1 by [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and has compact support in the same finite history interval: cone causality gives the upper bound, uniform subluminality gives the lower bound. Its derivative is F_s+z' dot grad_y F. Therefore the distributional Lorenz residual tested on the ORIGINAL SMOOTH psi equals
$$-\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}[z'(s)\cdot\nabla_yF(z(s),s)+F_s(z(s),s)]ds=0,$$
by [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], using c^-2/epsilon0=mu0. No derivative or cutoff is moved onto a noncompact distribution test. By [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]], finite coordinate cancellations give div curl0,curl grad0 and curl curl Upsilon=grad div Upsilon-Delta Upsilon. With G=div Upsilon+c^-2 Phi_t, direct algebra gives div mathcal E=W Phi-G_t and curl mathcal B-c^-2 mathcal E_t=W Upsilon+grad G. The two wave identities and G0 prove all four equations.
Locality and local integrability. A continuous regular distribution vanishing on an open set has its function identically zero: injectivity of [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]] gives zero almost everywhere, and a nonzero continuous value would give a nonzero neighborhood of positive measure by [[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]]. Thus classical derivative compatibility below also yields the four source-free classical equations off Gamma. The earlier lemma supplies regular Phi,Upsilon and C2 potentials on Q minus Gamma. Its C1 field formulas and the classical-compatibility clause of the distributional differentiation theorem give the stated restrictions. The graph is closed and null: each fixed-time spatial section is a singleton. The Borel graph is product-measurable by [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]], and [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] identifies product and Euclidean measure under the declared Countable Choice; hence Tonelli [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] gives zero four-dimensional measure. On any compact observation cylinder Q0, retarded s lies in [-S,t1], so A_Q=max_{[-S,t1]}|z''| is finite. With b*=v*/c, kappa>=1-b*, the explicit fields obey |E|+|B|<=C_Q(r^-2+r^-1), with constants depending on |q|,c,epsilon0,b*,A_Q, not on the individual observation point. The earlier C1 diffeomorphism g(s,y)=(z(s)+y,s+|y|/c) has absolute Jacobian kappa<=1+b*. The earlier proof establishes its global diffeomorphism property; the exact [[lem-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-borel-functions-via-radon-uniqueness]], under the declared Countable Choice, gives
$$\int_{Q_0}r^{-p}dxdt\le(1+b_*)(t_1+S)_+\int_{B_L}|y|^{-p}dy<\infty\qquad(p=1,2).$$
The last integrals are 4pi L²/2 and 4pi L respectively. Thus zero-extended classical E,B are L1loc; this alone is not yet identification across Gamma.
No hidden curve delta in the first potential derivatives. Put d=|x-z(t)|. Since t-s=r/c and |z(t)-z(s)|<=b*r, one has (1-b*)r<=d<=(1+b*)r. Potentials are consequently bounded by C/d on each compact observation cylinder. Choose a smooth spatial cutoff chi on R³, zero on B1 and one outside B2, with bounded derivative ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]); set chi_epsilon(x,t)=chi((x-z(t))/epsilon). This is C3, sufficient for CLASSICAL C1 integration by parts, but it need not be a C-infinity distribution test. Its spatial gradients are bounded by C/epsilon, its time derivative by Cv*/epsilon, and all are supported on epsilon<=d<=2epsilon. Ordinary compact C1 products with the original psi can be integrated by parts in each coordinate via [[thm-integration-by-parts]], followed by finite rectangle Fubini and [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]] under the declared Countable Choice; equivalently extend chi_epsilon times each potential by zero, which is C1 across its vanished neighborhood. For any first spatial or time derivative D, the resulting ordinary integral identity is
$$\int \chi_\epsilon(Df)\psi=-\int \chi_\epsilon f D\psi-\int f(D\chi_\epsilon)\psi,$$
where f is any potential component off Gamma. On the cutoff shell |f|<=C/epsilon, |Dchi_epsilon|<=C'/epsilon. Spatial translations give shell volume O(epsilon³) at each t ([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]), and the time interval of psi is fixed; the last integral is O(epsilon). Since f and its classical first derivatives are L1loc (the latter also follow directly from the earlier D-gradient and D_t formulas with bounded compact-history acceleration), dominated convergence lets epsilon tend0 in the first two integrals. It gives -integral f Dpsi=integral (Df)psi for each ORIGINAL smooth psi. Hence global distributional first derivatives have exactly the locally integrable classical representatives, and their finite combinations identify mathcal E,mathcal B with zero-extended E,B. No product of distributions, singular-field value, stronger worldline regularity, or noncompact test action enters.

items.title: Explicit checks of the retarded kernel, the static Liénard-Wiechert specialization and an explicit Lorenz-gauge transformation
items.reference: batch-21-local-construction (see research/physics-em-sr-40-2026-10-08-batch-21.notes.md); the design reserves no example for this B page, and this example checks lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel(a), lem-em-gauge-wave-reachability(b)-(c) and lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields(c) in explicit instances
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. (i) Static specialization. Take $z\equiv0$ (so $v_*=0$), $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, in the setting of [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]]. Then for $x\ne0$ the root is $s=t-|x|/c$, $r=|x|$, $n=x/|x|$, $\beta=0$, $\kappa=1$, $\dot\beta=0$, so the potentials and fields are $\varphi=C/|x|$, $A=0$, $E=C\,x/|x|^3$, $B=0$. Thus the retarded formulas reduce exactly to the Coulomb field with the convention $C=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and the kernel's explicit retarded-history integral reproduces the time-independent Poisson kernel $1/(4\pi|x-y|)$: for a static spatial source $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, define the all-time retarded extension by
$$u(x,t):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{h(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy.$$
Indeed the retarded time is $t-|x-y|/c$ and evaluating the static source there leaves $h(y)$ unchanged. This finite integral is the extension of the compact spacetime-source formula by source-time cutoffs on each compact observation region; a time-independent nonzero source is not itself compactly supported in spacetime. (ii) Explicit Lorenz-gauge transformation. On $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ take $\varphi\equiv0$ and $A(x,t)=(x_1,0,0)$. Then $G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A=1$ and $E=-\partial_tA=0$, $B=\operatorname{curl}A=0$. The quadratic function $\chi(x,t):=-|x|^2/6$ satisfies $W\chi=G$: indeed $\partial_t^2\chi=0$ and $\Delta\chi=-1$, so $W\chi=c^{-2}\cdot0-(-1)=1=G$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]). Its gauge transform is $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(0,\ ((2/3)x_1,-x_2/3,-x_3/3))$, which satisfies $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=\frac23-\frac13-\frac13=0$ and has the same fields: $E(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=0=E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=0=B(\varphi,A)$. This checks clauses (b) and (c) of [[lem-em-gauge-wave-reachability]] in an instance where $G$ is a nonzero constant and where the gauge function does not have the zero Cauchy data used in the existence construction of that lemma; by its clause (d), the difference of this $\chi$ and the zero-data solution of $W\chi=G$ solves the homogeneous wave equation, which is why both may be used. (iii) Sharpness of the kernel support at the apex. For a nonnegative $\psi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$ with $\psi(0,0)>0$ one has $\langle K,\psi\rangle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\psi(y,|y|/c)|y|^{-1}dy>0$, so $(0,0)\in\operatorname{supp}K$ and the apex is not an artefact of the definition; the same computation with a bump near $(y_0,|y_0|/c)$, $y_0\ne0$, shows that every point of the cone is in the support. These are mathematical checks of the pair's conventions and hypotheses; no measurement, physical field identification, or empirical claim is made.
